Microplastic Influx into Arable Soils via Sewage Sludge and Mulch Degradation

Author: Dr. Beatrice Ramos | October 5, 2025 | Agro-Ecosystems Section

Pathways of Soil Contamination

Agricultural soils represent a massive, long-term terrestrial sink for synthetic polymer fragments, often containing orders of magnitude higher plastic mass per hectare than oceanic surface gyres. The primary entry routes into arable topsoils are the land application of municipal wastewater sewage sludge (biosolids) as fertilizer and the extensive use of low-density polyethylene (LDPE) agricultural plasticulture mulch films.

Spectroscopic FTIR and Py-GC/MS soil core analyses across intensively farmed test plots revealed microplastic concentrations ranging from 12,000 to 67,500 particles per kilogram of dry topsoil. Fragmented mulch films degrade under solar ultraviolet radiation and tillage friction into secondary micro- and nanoplastics with mean particle diameters under 50 micrometers.

Impact on Soil Physical Properties and Microbial Biomass

Elevated microplastic residues alter bulk soil density, reduce hydraulic conductivity by 22%, and increase water-stable aggregate breakdown. Furthermore, the presence of hydrophobic plastic surfaces creates artificial 'plastisphere' niches that select for opportunistic pathogens while suppressing native nitrogen-fixing rhizobia bacteria and reducing earthworm (Lumbricus terrestris) juvenile growth rates by 34%.
